focus_areas: IssueRepository (issue search) — free-text query into a SQL command
AttachmentService (attachment download) — route name into a file path
ReportExporter (report export) — export params into an external process
BackupService (restore) — request body into a deserializer
PasswordHasher (registration) — password into a hashing routine

findings.title: SQL injection via string-concatenated LIKE clause in issue search
findings.description: Search() builds CommandText by concatenating the untrusted `query` argument directly into a SQL string: "... WHERE title LIKE '%" + query + "%' ...". `query` is the `q` value from GET /issues/search (Program.cs:25). No parameterization or escaping. An attacker closes the string literal and injects arbitrary SQL.
findings.exploit_scenario: GET /issues/search?q=' OR 1=1-- returns every row regardless of the intended LIKE filter; a UNION SELECT extracts arbitrary data (e.g. sqlite_version(), other tables).
findings.recommendation: Use a parameterized query: command.CommandText = "... WHERE title LIKE @q ..."; command.Parameters.AddWithValue("@q", "%" + query + "%").
findings.confidence_reason: Textbook string-concatenated SQL with directly attacker-controlled input reaching ExecuteReader.

findings.title: OS command injection via unsanitized label in /bin/sh -c argument
findings.description: Export() constructs a shell command by concatenating the untrusted `label` (and `format`) into an Arguments string executed by /bin/sh -c: "-c \"pandoc -t " + format + " -o /tmp/report_" + label + ".out\"". Both fields come from the POST /reports/export JSON body (Program.cs:32). Shell metacharacters in `label`/`format` break out of the intended command.
findings.exploit_scenario: POST /reports/export with label = "x; id; touch /tmp/pwned #" runs `id` (and any command) as the server user; stdout is returned in the HTTP response.
findings.recommendation: Do not build a shell string from input. Invoke the converter directly with an argument array (no /bin/sh), and validate `format` against an allowlist. Reject or escape `label`.
findings.confidence_reason: Direct concatenation of request input into a /bin/sh -c command line.

findings.title: Insecure deserialization: Newtonsoft TypeNameHandling.All on untrusted body
findings.description: Restore() deserializes the raw request body with SerializerSettings { TypeNameHandling = TypeNameHandling.All } (line 10), applied in JsonConvert.DeserializeObject at line 17. TypeNameHandling.All honors an attacker-supplied `$type`, letting the request choose which .NET types are constructed. Body is POST /backups/restore (Program.cs:36).
findings.exploit_scenario: A `$type` gadget payload instantiates arbitrary types; with a suitable gadget chain present in the process this yields remote code execution. Even without a weaponized gadget, attacker-chosen types are instantiated from the wire.
findings.recommendation: Set TypeNameHandling = TypeNameHandling.None (the default) and deserialize into a known DTO, or use System.Text.Json. Never deserialize untrusted input with polymorphic type handling.
findings.confidence_reason: TypeNameHandling.All on attacker-controlled input is a well-known RCE-class primitive.

findings.title: Hardcoded pepper embedded in source
findings.description: PasswordHasher hardcodes `private const Pepper = "s3cr3t-pepper-v1"` (line 9) and mixes it into every password hash (line 14). A secret compiled into source (and any repo/artifact) is known to anyone with read access and cannot be rotated per-deployment, so it provides no real protection.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker who reads the source (or decompiles the assembly) knows the pepper, so it adds zero entropy to offline cracking of any leaked hash.
findings.recommendation: Load the pepper from a secret store / environment at runtime; never commit it. Combine with a per-user random salt.
findings.confidence_reason: Literal secret assigned to a const and used in the hash.

findings.title: Weak password hashing: unsalted fast MD5
findings.description: Hash() derives the stored password representation with MD5 (line 13-14). MD5 is fast and collision-broken, and here it is used with only a static pepper and no per-user salt or work factor, making stored hashes cheap to brute-force / rainbow-table.
findings.exploit_scenario: Given a leaked hash, an attacker recovers weak passwords with a wordlist in milliseconds (MD5(guess + known pepper)).
findings.recommendation: Use a memory-hard password KDF (Argon2id, scrypt, or PBKDF2 with a high iteration count) and a per-user random salt.
findings.confidence_reason: MD5.Create() used for password storage — unambiguous weak-hash pattern.

findings.title: Path traversal / absolute-path override in attachment read
findings.description: Read() builds a filesystem path with Path.Combine(_storageRoot, name) (line 12) and passes it straight to File.ReadAllBytes (line 13). `name` is the untrusted route segment from GET /attachments/{name} (Program.cs:28). Path.Combine performs no containment check: a '../' sequence escapes the storage root, and an absolute `name` causes Path.Combine to discard `_storageRoot` entirely.
findings.exploit_scenario: GET /attachments/..%2f..%2f..%2fetc%2fpasswd (or an absolute name) is intended to read files outside the storage root. NOTE for triage: reachability depends on the HTTP stack decoding %2f into a real '/' for a single-segment {name} route — default Kestrel does not, which neutralizes this specific trigger (see live-verification report).
findings.recommendation: Resolve the combined path (Path.GetFullPath) and verify it is still under _storageRoot before reading; reject names containing path separators or '..'.
findings.confidence_reason: Classic Path.Combine + ReadAllBytes with no containment check; the code-level flaw is real even though the default-Kestrel HTTP trigger is mitigated by route binding.

findings.title: No authentication or authorization on any endpoint
findings.description: All five endpoints (search, attachment download, report export, backup restore, register) are mapped with no authentication or authorization middleware. Every sink above is reachable by any unauthenticated caller.
findings.exploit_scenario: Any of the injection/traversal/deserialization sinks is reachable anonymously; there is no trust gate in front of them.
findings.recommendation: Add authentication + authorization appropriate to the deployment; treat all five endpoints as sensitive.
findings.confidence_reason: Observation, not a discrete sink; noted as an amplifier for the other findings (the THREAT_MODEL declares auth out of scope).
